name: Caudate nucleus
func: A C-shaped nucleus of the basal ganglia curving alongside the lateral ventricle. It helps choose and start actions, learn from rewards and form habits, and links planning areas of the frontal lobe to movement.

levels.kid:
The **caudate nucleus** is a curvy part deep in your brain shaped like a **tadpole**, with a big head and a long, thin tail. "Caudate" means "having a tail"!

It wraps around a fluid-filled space in the middle of your brain.

The caudate helps you **pick what to do next** and learn from what happens. If you try a new game and win a prize, the caudate helps you remember, "That was good, do it again!"

It also helps turn things you practice a lot into **habits**, like brushing your teeth every night without even thinking about it.
levels.hs:
The **caudate nucleus** is one of the **basal ganglia**, a group of deep gray-matter nuclei that help control movement and behavior. It is a C-shaped structure with three parts:

- The big **head**, which bulges into the **frontal horn of the lateral ventricle**, forming its side wall.
- The **body**, which runs back along the side of the lateral ventricle, above and lateral to the **thalamus**.
- The thin **tail**, which curves down into the temporal lobe and forward in the roof of the **temporal horn**, ending near the **amygdala**.

Between the caudate (on the inside) and the **lentiform nucleus** (putamen and globus pallidus, on the outside) runs the **anterior limb of the internal capsule**, a thick band of nerve fibers. Many thin gray bridges cross this band and connect the caudate head to the putamen, giving the area its striped look. That is why the caudate and putamen together are called the **striatum** ("striped body").

At the bottom front, the caudate head merges with the putamen at the **nucleus accumbens**, part of the brain's reward system.

**What it does:** the caudate receives signals mostly from the **prefrontal cortex** and helps with goal-directed behavior, planning, learning from rewards and mistakes, and switching between tasks. It depends on **dopamine** from the midbrain to work properly.
levels.college:
The caudate and putamen share the same cell types and connections and form the **dorsal striatum**; the **nucleus accumbens** and olfactory tubercle form the **ventral striatum**. The **stria terminalis** and the **thalamostriate vein** run in the groove between the caudate body and thalamus.

**Inputs:**
- **Cortex** (glutamate): the caudate receives mainly from **association cortex**, including dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, orbitofrontal cortex, frontal eye fields and posterior parietal cortex, while the putamen receives mostly sensorimotor cortex.
- **Substantia nigra pars compacta** (dopamine) via the **nigrostriatal pathway**.
- **Intralaminar thalamus** (centromedian and parafascicular nuclei).

**Outputs:** striatal neurons project to the **globus pallidus** and **substantia nigra pars reticulata**, which then influence the thalamus (VA, VL and mediodorsal nuclei), which projects back to cortex, completing the loop.

**Parallel loops:** the caudate is part of the **dorsolateral prefrontal loop** (executive function), the **lateral orbitofrontal loop** (behavior regulation) and the **oculomotor loop** (frontal eye fields; caudate body to SNr to superior colliculus, controlling saccades).

**Blood supply:**
- The **medial lenticulostriate arteries** from the ACA and the **recurrent artery of Heubner**, usually arising near the ACA-ACom junction, supply the caudate head and the anterior limb of the internal capsule.
- The **lateral lenticulostriate arteries** from the MCA supply the body.
- The **anterior choroidal artery** supplies the tail.

**Veins:** the **anterior caudate veins** and thalamostriate vein drain to the internal cerebral veins.
levels.phd:
**Cell types:** about 95% of striatal neurons are GABAergic **medium spiny neurons (MSNs)**, covered in dendritic spines where cortical glutamate and nigral dopamine inputs meet. They come in two main types:
- **D1-receptor MSNs** (also expressing substance P and dynorphin) form the **direct pathway**, projecting to GPi/SNr.
- **D2-receptor MSNs** (expressing enkephalin) form the **indirect pathway**, projecting to GPe.

The rest are interneurons: **cholinergic interneurons** (tonically active neurons that pause in response to rewarding cues), **parvalbumin-positive fast-spiking** GABAergic interneurons and others.

**Compartments:** the striatum is organized into **striosomes (patches)** and **matrix**, defined by markers such as mu-opioid receptors. Striosomes receive more limbic input and project to dopamine neurons, while the matrix handles sensorimotor and associative input (Graybiel).

**Dopamine and learning:** dopamine neurons signal **reward prediction errors**: firing increases for unexpectedly good outcomes and dips for worse-than-expected ones (Schultz). In the striatum, dopamine strengthens or weakens corticostriatal synapses through **spike-timing-dependent plasticity** that depends on D1 or D2 receptors, which is a biological form of reinforcement learning.

**Goal-directed vs habitual:** the **dorsomedial striatum** (the caudate in primates) supports **goal-directed** action sensitive to outcome value, while the **dorsolateral striatum** (putamen) supports **habits** (Balleine, Yin). As training continues, control shifts from caudate to putamen. Devaluing a reward stops goal-directed actions but not well-learned habits.

**Selection:** a classic view (Redgrave, Prescott, Gurney) holds that the basal ganglia act as a central "selector," releasing one action while suppressing competing ones.
levels.expert:
**Huntington disease:** an autosomal dominant **CAG trinucleotide repeat** expansion in the **HTT gene** (40 or more repeats is fully penetrant; 36–39 has reduced penetrance). Indirect-pathway (D2/enkephalin) MSNs in the caudate are lost early, which reduces inhibition of movement and causes **chorea**: irregular, flowing, dance-like movements. Patients also develop cognitive decline, psychiatric changes and motor impersistence (cannot keep the tongue out, "milkmaid's grip"). Larger expansions cause earlier onset, and repeats can expand when passed down through generations (**anticipation**). MRI shows **caudate atrophy**, with "**boxcar**" ventricles because the frontal horns lose their normal inward bulge. Treatments manage symptoms; gene-silencing therapies are under study.

**Other conditions:**
- **Sydenham chorea**: an autoimmune reaction after streptococcal infection (rheumatic fever) in children.
- **Caudate infarcts** (from Heubner's artery or lenticulostriate occlusion): abulia, apathy, confusion and sometimes disinhibition, often more than weakness.
- **Wilson disease:** copper buildup in the basal ganglia (with Kayser-Fleischer rings in the cornea and liver disease).
- **Neuroacanthocytosis** and **benign hereditary chorea** are rarer causes.
- **Obsessive-compulsive disorder** imaging shows abnormal activity in orbitofrontal-caudate loops, though this is a group finding rather than a test.

**Surgical anatomy:** the caudate head forms the lateral wall of the frontal horn. During **transcallosal or endoscopic** approaches, the **foramen of Monro** is identified by following the **thalamostriate vein** and choroid plexus; the caudate lies lateral and in front. A **ventriculostomy (EVD)** catheter is aimed at the frontal horn just medial to the caudate head, at **Kocher's point**. A **caudate hemorrhage** often ruptures into the ventricle and can cause hydrocephalus. **Germinal matrix hemorrhage** in premature babies arises at the caudothalamic groove.

keyPoints: C-shaped: head, body, tail; follows the lateral ventricle
Head forms the lateral wall of the frontal horn
Separated from the putamen by the anterior limb of the internal capsule
Caudate + putamen = striatum; input from association (prefrontal) cortex
Medium spiny neurons; direct (D1) and indirect (D2) pathways
Huntington disease → caudate atrophy and chorea

test.q: The head of the caudate forms the lateral wall of which space?
choices: Frontal horn of the lateral ventricle
test.explain: The caudate head bulges into the frontal (anterior) horn.

test.q: The caudate and putamen together are called the ______.
test.explain: Gray bridges across the internal capsule give them a striped look.

test.q: Which artery classically supplies the caudate head and anterior limb of the internal capsule?
test.explain: Heubner's artery usually arises near the ACA-ACom junction.
MSNs are the main input and output neurons of the striatum.

test.q: Huntington disease is caused by an expanded ______ repeat in the HTT gene.
test.explain: CAG encodes glutamine, producing a polyglutamine tract.

test.q: On MRI, Huntington disease classically shows:
test.explain: Loss of the caudate's bulge into the frontal horns gives a boxcar shape.
